The role of endogenous toxins from cellular oxidative reac-
tions has emerged because aging has been associated with a loss 
of neurons containing dopamine and an increase in monoamine 
oxidase. When metabolized (enzymatic oxidation and autoxida-
tion), dopamine produces endogenous toxins (hydrogen perox-
ide and free radicals), causing peroxidation of membrane lipids 
and cell death. In the presence of an inherited or acquired predis-
position, severe oxidative injury can lead to substantial loss of 
dopaminergic neurons similar to that observed in PD.
Several other environmental factors also have been impli-
cated as causal factors of PD. The connection between smoking 
and a lowered risk for PD has been evaluated, but results are 
inconsistent (Ma et al, 2006). In older patients, drug-induced 
PD may occur as a side effect of neuroleptics or metoclo-
pramide (see Chapter 8 and Appendix 23).
Dairy products have been linked to PD (Jiang et al, 2014). 
A meta-analysis of dairy intake and PD risk found a 17% in-
crease in PD for every 200 g/day increment in milk intake.
